h1: Eisbock explained: the strong lager made by freezing
title: Eisbock: The Lager Made by Freezing | Craft Beer School
desc: What eisbock is, how freezing turns a doppelbock into a 9 to 14% lager, what it tastes like, the legend behind it and how to serve it.
teaser: Freeze a strong lager, take out the ice and what is left is stronger, sweeter and darker. That is eisbock.
standfirst: Eisbock is one of the strangest beers in the German tradition: a strong lager made even stronger by freezing it and removing the ice. Here is how it works, what it tastes like and why you should not try it at home.
sections:
Eisbock means ice bock. It starts as a strong dark lager, usually a doppelbock, which is then partly frozen. Water freezes before alcohol does, so brewers remove the ice crystals and leave behind a smaller volume of beer with more alcohol, more sugar and more flavour packed into it.

The BJCP gives eisbock a range of roughly 9 to 14% ABV, deep copper to dark brown, with low bitterness. Our guide to bock and doppelbock explains the beers it is made from.

The usual story places eisbock in Kulmbach, in northern Bavaria. A brewery worker supposedly left barrels of bock outside on a winter night. The beer partly froze and split the barrels. Rather than waste it, the brewers tasted the liquid trapped inside the ice and found it stronger and richer than the original.

Like many brewing origin stories, it is hard to verify. What is certain is that Kulmbach and Franconia are strongly associated with the style and that cold winters made the process possible long before refrigeration.

Water freezes at 0 °C. A solution of ethanol and sugar freezes at a lower temperature. When brewers chill a doppelbock to a few degrees below zero, pure water ice forms first. Removing that ice leaves a liquid with a higher concentration of everything else: alcohol, residual sugar, colour, proteins and flavour compounds.

Brewers decide how much ice to remove. Taking out a tenth of the volume raises the strength a little. Taking out a quarter or more pushes it towards the top of the range. Because the process concentrates rather than creates alcohol, an eisbock tastes very different from a beer simply fermented to the same strength.

A clear lager base matters. Concentration magnifies everything, including any off flavours. A doppelbock with a little diacetyl or sulphur becomes an eisbock with a lot of it. That is why the base beer needs a long, cold lagering period first.

Eisbock is rich, smooth and warming. Expect dark fruit such as plum, raisin and fig, with deep caramel, toffee and bread crust from Munich malt. Alcohol shows as warmth but should be smooth, never hot or solvent like. Bitterness is low and carbonation moderate to low.

The body is full and the sweetness noticeable, but a good eisbock finishes clean rather than syrupy. It sits closer in feel to a fortified wine than to a typical lager. Comparisons with a malt led English barleywine are fair, though eisbock is cleaner because it is lager fermented.
Eisbock, ice beer and the law

Freeze concentration also explains ice beer, a 1990s mass market trend where breweries partly froze lager to remove a little water. The change was small compared with eisbock and the beers stayed light.

A word of caution. Concentrating alcohol by freezing can count as a form of distillation in some legal systems. Home brewing itself has a complicated legal status in India that varies by state. Do not try to freeze concentrate beer at home. Commercial eisbock is made under licence. The rules about it differ by country and change over time.

Serve eisbock in a small snifter or tulip glass at about 10 to 14 °C. Cold dulls its richness. Pour 100 to 150 ml and sip it slowly. A single bottle can serve three or four people.

It works as an after dinner drink with dark chocolate, plum cake, blue cheese or a dense dessert. In India, try it with a small piece of kaju katli or a gur based sweet. Its malt sweetness meets the jaggery or nut flavours well.

Eisbock is rare in India because it is costly to make and import. If you find one, buy two: drink one now and keep one in cool storage for a year. Like other strong dark beers, it develops sherry and dried fruit notes with time.
Why the style is worth knowing

Eisbock sits at the edge of what beer can be. Understanding it means understanding how lager strength, malt, temperature and concentration interact. It is also a reminder that many beer styles grew from accidents and climates rather than design. Tracing those roots across the German lager family, from helles to eisbock, is one of the more rewarding ways to learn beer.
faqs: Roughly 9 to 14% ABV. The strength depends on how much ice the brewer removes.
Can I make eisbock at home?
We do not recommend it. Freeze concentration can count as distillation under some laws. Home brewing rules also in India vary by state.
What is the difference between eisbock and doppelbock?
Eisbock is a doppelbock that has been partly frozen with the ice removed, making it stronger, richer and sweeter.
